draft.title: Direct proportion and scale
card: Two quantities are in direct proportion when one is always the same multiple of the other. If one doubles, so does the other. The multiple is called the constant of proportion.
To find the constant, divide one quantity by the other. If 4 pens cost $6, the constant is 6 ÷ 4 = $1.50 per pen. Then 10 pens cost 10 × 1.50 = $15.
A scale drawing is a direct proportion. A scale of 1 cm to 2 m means every 1 cm on the drawing stands for 2 m in real life.
To find a real length, multiply the drawing length by the real length for 1 cm. To find a drawing length, divide the real length by it. Check that the units match.
draft.remember: In direct proportion, one quantity is always the same multiple of the other. A scale is one example.

a.q: A plan has a scale of 1 cm to 2 m. A deck is 7 cm long on the plan. What is its real length?
a.why: Each 1 cm stands for 2 m, so 7 cm stands for 7 × 2 = 14 m. Dividing 7 by 2 gives 3.5, which is the mistake of using the wrong operation for finding a real length.
a.clue: Each centimetre on the plan stands for 2 m.

b.q: Priya's map has a scale of 1 cm to 5 km. Two towns are 60 km apart in real life. How far apart are they on the map?
b.why: The map length is the real distance divided by the real length for 1 cm: 60 ÷ 5 = 12 cm. Multiplying gives 300, which would be right only for finding a real distance from the map.
b.clue: You start with the real distance and want the map distance.

problems.detail: The why says multiplying (60 × 5 = 300) 'would be right only for finding a real distance from the map'. That is misleading: finding a real distance multiplies the map length by 5, not the real distance. 60 × 5 is never a correct step, so the why could confuse students about when to multiply.

check.summary: Both questions are correct, with clear single answers (14 m and 12 cm). The only issue is a misleading line in the why for (b), which implies that multiplying 60 by 5 would be right when finding a real distance.
